───── ASSISTANT · 2026-08-27 00:04:28 ─────
Very good catch — both patterns are exactly the kind of thing that causes tools to either skip work silently or overwrite good data. Your two scenarios map to these rules, which I'm building in:

1. **`sub`/`subs`/`Subtitles` folders** adjacent to (or below) the video get scanned: any *detectably-English* file there marks the video covered; only foreign-language sets (e.g. just `Arabic.srt`) still trigger a download.
2. **Fake/stub `<name>.srt` sidecars** (typically 1–10 KB — often actually saved HTML error pages) stop counting as "covered": sidecars below a size threshold get content-verified (real cue timings + language script check) before being trusted. The real subs in the `subs` folder are then preferred. Downloads always land as `<name>.en.srt`, so genuine files are never overwritten.

## How it runs
```
node subtitles-fetcher.mjs status    progress dashboard
node subtitles-fetcher.mjs dry       peek at next N in queue
node subtitles-fetcher.mjs retry X   force-retry paths containing X
node subtitles-fetcher.mjs probe "…\movie.mkv"   debug one file
schedule 21:30 / --remove            manage the daily job
```
Each run stops exactly when SubDL's ~300/day cap trips (queue survives; resume tomorrow). At that pace: full coverage in **~6–7 weeks**, hands-free. Failed lookups park themselves after 3 tries so they don't clog the queue.

Every video in the library has a record that accumulates history across days:
```json
"aashiq banaya aapne….mkv": {
  "status": "done",          // covered | pending | failed | parked | done
  "provider": "sd",
  "rel": "Aashiq Banaya Aapne 2005 WebRip Hindi 720p ESub - mkvCinem",
  "when": "2026-08-27T07:42:11Z",
  "attempts": 1
}
```
Failed ones carry `lastError`, `attempts`, and `when` — which is how the retry/park logic knows when to stop trying a hopeless title.

# Plan delivered — `docs/plan-web-service.md` (pushed, `73eb5ea` + amendment)

## Key decisions in the plan

**Evolve, don't rebuild.** The irreplaceable value in this codebase isn't structure — it's the empirical scar tissue: SubDL's referer guard, Addic7ed's 302-vs-list duality, the underscore parser trap, fake-stub detection. A rewrite re-pays that tuition. So: Phase 0 extracts the proven core into `lib/` modules byte-identically, then the service grows around it. You get the new architecture without new risk.

**Your requirements, mapped:**
| You asked | Plan section |
|---|---|
| One `git clone` + single install command | `install.mjs` — interactive or flags, writes systemd unit (Linux) / boot scheduled task (Windows), health-checks, prints the LAN URL with token |
| Runs detached at startup like Jellyfin/qBittorrent | §7 — systemd `enable --now`; Windows `schtasks /SC ONSTART` (zero extra tools, NSSM documented as alternative) |
| LAN web UI, own port | default **:8097** (next to your 8090/8096), dark vanilla-JS dashboard, no build step |
| Pick movie & TV folders in UI | Folders tab with **server-side directory browser** (browsers can't browse the server's disks — the API can) |
| Status / reports / current activities | Dashboard tiles + **SSE live activity feed**; `/report` per-day charts; `activity.jsonl` append-only event log |
| Browse what it downloaded | Library tab: shows → seasons → episodes grid, movie grid |
| **Re-search & swap a subtitle** | The deepest API change: `/items/:key/candidates` lists ranked alternatives *without downloading*, one click swaps (old file kept as `.en.srt.1`, history records the swap) |
| Detached process | single long-running `service.mjs`; the listening port doubles as the instance lock; CLI becomes a remote control when the service is up |

**Security default:** LAN-bind + auto-generated token (installer prints the bookmark-ready URL) — usable from any device, useless to a nosy neighbor.

**Phases:** 0 extraction → 1 service+installer+dashboard → 2 folders/queue/settings → 3 library+swap → 4 reports. Each lands working software.

## Meanwhile, your desktop run today: mission accomplished then cap-hit

- **272 subtitles downloaded** today until SubDL's ~300/day allowance ran out
- Bonus discovery: the cap enforces as a **silent soft block** — pages come back 200-OK with results *stripped*, so misses masquerade as "no subtitles exist". I've already encoded the detection rule for Phase 1 into the plan (streak-detection + retroactive attempt-counter forgiveness)
- The run is still alive and now churning through remaining movies (harmless misses, auto-retry tomorrow) — once it reaches TV items, **Addic7ed kicks in unaffected** and keeps delivering tonight
- Tomorrow 13:05: fresh SubDL quota + the queue continues exactly where it stopped

When you're ready to build it, say the word and Phase 0 + 1 are the natural first swing — that alone gets you the service, installer, and dashboard on the M93p.

## What you got in this swing

**Engine intelligence (the important one):** the SubDL silent-cap behavior we discovered yesterday is now *handled in code* — after ~40 consecutive empty searches on a day with 100+ downloads, sd retires itself for the UTC day and every attempt it wasted during the streak is retroactively forgiven (re-queued, attempts refunded). Your old queue items that "failed" during yesterday's soft block will be re-attempted normally.

**Dashboard:** live activity feed (SSE), stat tiles, provider pills with quota, last-run card, **LAN URL card** (auto-detects the machine's LAN IP), and a **14-day downloads bar chart** with provider-share breakdown.

**Folders:** per-root reachability dots + covered/queued counts per folder.

**Item modal (queue + library):** status, release, errors, **history timeline**, park/un-park, re-queue, and the full **"Find alternatives" → swap** flow (providers searched live, one click downloads & swaps, old subtitle kept as `.srt.1`).

**Settings:** behavior toggles, provider order, schedule, OpenSubtitles credentials, and **access-token regeneration** (old token stays valid until restart so you can't lock yourself out).

───── ASSISTANT · 2026-08-28 15:40:35 ─────
Fixed, pushed (`git log: fix: empty modal was stuck open`). **Do one hard refresh — Ctrl+F5** — and the whole dashboard appears underneath; it was there all along.

**Root cause:** CSS specificity footgun. The stylesheet set `#modal { display:flex }`, which outranks the browser's built-in `[hidden] { display:none }` rule. So the hidden attribute on the overlay was ignored — an empty modal with a lone Close button covered the page from the moment it loaded, and clicking Close *did* set `hidden=true`… which the CSS kept overriding. The UI underneath never had a chance.

**What changed:**
- `#modal[hidden] { display:none }` — the toggle now actually works
- Clicking the dark backdrop or pressing **Escape** also closes it
- Static files now serve with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, so future fixes reach your browser on a normal refresh instead of needing cache-busting

No service restart was needed — static files are read from disk per request, so the corrected CSS/JS are already being served. Your fetch engine kept working through all of this (it's server-side); the queue has been moving the whole time.

───── ASSISTANT · 2026-08-28 15:45:38 ─────
Both done and live. **Refresh the page (F5)** for the feed fix; the service is already running the new engine.

## 1. Feed scroll — fixed
The feed now appends lines instead of rebuilding, and auto-scrolls **only while you're already at the bottom** (48px threshold). Scroll up and it stays put; scroll back to the bottom and it pins again. It also backfills the last 60 events on page load so you land on recent history.

## 2. The logic — your understanding is ~90% right

```
per video:  try a7 → try sd → try os (inactive until you add a free key)
   movie :  a7 skips it by design  →  SubDL does the work
episode :  Addic7ed first (release-team matched, community-synced)
           if a7 lacks it → SubDL → (OS later)
```

- **SubDL**: ~**300 downloads/day per IP**, shared by everything that reaches it. Plus the nastiness we discovered: when exhausted it doesn't error — it serves empty results silently. The engine now detects that streak, retires sd for the rest of the UTC day, and forgives the attempts it wasted.
- **Addic7ed**: no numeric daily cap — **but "no limit" ≠ "no rules."** It throttles hard when hammered, so we pace every a7 request ~3.2 s apart and cool down when it complains. Practically that's a ceiling of ~1,000/hour, and we deliberately stay human-paced. So yes — **TV effectively runs 24/7**, as it did last night (~940 subs in an evening).

**The flaw you almost caught:** queue order runs movies (a→z) before TV — and once SubDL's day ended, every remaining *movie* still got tried daily, failed instantly (a7 skips movies), burned its 3 attempts, and **parked permanently**. That's the opposite of what you'd want. Fixed just now:

> **New rule:** if no source can serve an item today, it's **deferred — zero attempts spent**. So tonight the engine zoomed past the remaining movies (no penalty) and went straight to living on Addic7ed TV episodes all night. Movies resume automatically when SubDL's quota resets.

Restarted the service to activate all this — verified: engine `fetching`, currently on a Bengali series (`aaj robibar S01E02`), with sd-capped movies being cleanly deferred behind it.

## What was wrong

1. **Adventure Time's poster**: the art resolver only checked the *episode's own folder* for TV — Adventure Time keeps its `folder.jpg` in the show folder above. Now TV art walks **episode dir → show dir → grandparent**, and poster requests may fall back to `backdrop.jpg`/`fanart.jpg` when no portrait art exists (your "show either" rule). Verified: Adventure Time now serves its 247KB `folder.jpg`. *(The "Adenture" spelling is in the actual folder name on the NAS — Jellyfin matches it fine either way.)*

2. **OMDB posters now persist into your library**: when local art is missing and an OMDB key is configured, the fetched poster is downloaded and saved **into the show/movie folder as `poster.jpg`** (backdrops as `backdrop.jpg`) — so Jellyfin picks it up too, not just this dashboard. Magic-byte validated, never overwrites existing files, and the fetch failure path still falls back to hot-linking so the UI always shows something. Add your free key in *Settings → Poster art fallback* to activate.

3. **Lowercase titles, root-caused**: items restored from the v1 era had no cached metadata, and the scanner only backfilled metadata when a file's mtime changed — so most items were permanently falling back to their lowercase path key. The scanner now **always backfills** metadata (a rescan is running in the background to fill it all in), and the display layer additionally prettifies show names, so everything reads "Adventure Time" regardless.

4. **Tab switching hardened**: bindings restructured with error toasts — if anything breaks client-side again, you'll see a red toast with the actual message instead of silent dead buttons.

1. **Working as designed per-item**: each priority POST = one mini-run downloading that episode immediately alongside the scan. 3 episodes verified downloaded to the NAS.

async priorityRequest(key) {
  const k = key.toLowerCase();
  const rec = state.files[k];
  if (rec && (rec.status === "done" || rec.status === "covered"))
    return { queued: false, note: "Already has an English subtitle — use "Find alternatives" to swap it." };
  if (rec) { rec.status = "pending"; rec.attempts = 0; persist(); }
  prioritySet.add(k);
  this.drainPriority();            // fire-and-forget
  return { queued: true, mode: this.phase === "fetching" ? "next-in-run" : "immediate" };
},

/** background drain: keeps a scoped runner alive while the priority set is non-empty */
drainPriority() {
  if (this.phase === "fetching") return;   // main run will takePriority() itself
  if (miniRunning) return;                 // loop already alive
  miniRunning = true;
  (async () => {
    try {
      while (prioritySet.size > 0) {
        const batch = [...prioritySet]; prioritySet.clear();
        pushActivity({ ev: "priority", key: batch[0], count: batch.length });
        await runFetch(cfg, state, {
          onlySub: batch.join("\u0000"),  // hmm — how does onlySub work? need to check
          saveState: persist,
          takePriority: () => { const ks = [...prioritySet]; prioritySet.clear(); return ks; },
          onEvent: (e) => { pushActivity(e); web.broadcast(e); },
        });
      }
    } finally { miniRunning = false; }
  })();
},
```

# Done — the count cards are now real-time (pushed, `276f079`)

Your instinct was exactly right: the live feed runs on **SSE** (Server-Sent Events — a one-way push channel, no polling, no websocket), and it now carries the dashboard state too.

## How it works

| Side | Change |
|---|---|
| **Server** | Every engine event (download, miss, scan progress, run end, park…) now also emits a throttled status snapshot (max 1 per 2 s) through the same SSE channel — and the scheduler pushes one every 30 s so even quiet periods stay fresh |
| **Client** | The `EventSource` handler recognizes `status` frames and re-renders the tiles, engine phase dot, provider pills, and last-run line through the same render function the page load uses — the activity feed itself is untouched |
| **Chart** | The 14-day chart only re-pulls when the covered count actually moves (not on every frame) |

## Verified live

Sampled the raw SSE stream: `status` frames arrive with the full payload — and watching them you can see the scan working right now: **covered jumped 5,557 → 6,303** as the scheduler-injected scan re-credits files that already have sidecars. After the scan finishes, tv247 resumes automatically.

Improvements to make:
1. **Replace the recursive readdir with a manual iterative walk** that emits progress DURING the walk (directories visited / files found). This gives true realtime "walking" feedback and eliminates the long silent buffering phase. **scanner.mjs — `refreshInventoryAsync`:**
```js
async function walkRootAsync(root, videos, onWalk) {
  const queue = [root];
  let dirs = 0;
  while (queue.length) {
    const dir = queue.shift();
    let entries;
    try { entries = await fs.promises.readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true }); }
    catch (e) { console.error(`walk: readdir failed (${e.message}): ${dir}`); continue; }
    for (const ent of entries) {
      const full = dir.endsWith("\\") || dir.endsWith("/") ? dir + ent.name : dir + path.sep + ent.name;  // careful with separators; use path.join(dir, ent.name)
      if (ent.isDirectory()) {
        if (/^[\.@]?trickplay$/i.test(ent.name) || ent.name === ".actors" ...) continue;  // keep existing trickplay skip logic at file level; dirs: skip .trickplay subtree
        queue.push(full);
      } else if (ent.isFile()) {
        if (!VIDEO_EXTS.has(path.extname(ent.name).toLowerCase())) continue;
        const n = norm(full);
        if (/(^|\/)\.trickplay(\/|$)/i.test(n)) continue;
        videos.push(n);
      }
    }
    dirs++;
    onWalk?.(dir, videos.length, queue.length);
  }
}
```
- Skip junk dirs to save time: `.trickplay` (Jellyfin thumbs — HUGE subtree with thousands of image files!), `.actors`, `extrafanart`? Careful: the current code skips files under `.trickplay` paths. With a manual walk I can prune `.trickplay`/`extras`? directories entirely — big speedup (trickplay dirs contain hundreds of images each — currently they're walked and filtered file-by-file).
  - Keep semantics: prune directories named `.trickplay` (case-insensitive) — matches existing filter `/(^|\/)\.trickplay(\/|$)/i`. Also maybe `.@__thumb`? Don't over-engineer: prune `.trickplay` only (plus keep the path filter for safety).

Actually simpler: write a small module-level `queueLabel(k, r)`:
```js
function queueLabel(k, r) {
  const meta = r.meta;
  if (meta?.kind === "episode" && meta.show && meta.show !== "$1") {
    return `${prettyTitle(meta.show)} · S${String(meta.season).padStart(2, "0")}E${String(meta.episode).padStart(2, "0")}`;
  }
  // raw-path fallback: show folder under "TV Series" + episode number from the file
  const segs = k.split("/").filter(Boolean);
  const tvIdx = segs.findIndex(s => /^tv[\s._-]*series$/i.test(s));
  const showSeg = tvIdx >= 0 ? segs[tvIdx + 1] : segs[segs.length - 2] ?? "";
  let name = showSeg.replace(/\((?:19|20)\d{2}(?:\s*[-–—]\s*(?:19|20)\d{2})?\)/g, "")
    .replace(/\bseason[s]?\b.*$|\bs\d{1,2}\b.*$/i, "").replace(/[._]/g, " ").replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
  name = name ? prettyTitle(name) : "";
  if (!name) name = prettyTitle(decodeURIComponent(k.split("/").pop().replace(/\.[^.]+$/, "")));
  const se = /s(\d{1,2})[\s._-]*e(\d{1,4})/i.exec(k);
  return name + (se ? ` · S${se[1].padStart(2, "0")}E${se[2].padStart(2, "0")}` : "");
}
```
For movies (kind movie or unknown): use meta title + year like library:

    const title = prettyTitle(meta?.title || k.split("/").pop().replace(/\.[^.]+$/, ""));
    return meta?.year ? `${title} (${meta.year})` : title;
  }
```

# Analysis + fixes (pushed, `491378d`)

## Where the "old data" comes from

There are two layers, and the staleness was client-side:

1. **Server**: `/api/queue` reads **live** from the in-memory ledger (`state.files`) — the same store the engine and scanner mutate. It's never stale on the server.
2. **Client**: `loadQueue()` fetched **exactly once, when you opened the tab**, and only re-fetched on Filter/pagination clicks. Everything since that fetch — downloads, status flips, the scan's reclassification — was invisible. With the tiles now updating in real time via SSE, the frozen queue next to them stood out as "old data."
3. There's also a legitimate subtlety: during the walk, the scanner updates each record only when it reaches that file. Rows it hasn't re-verified yet show their *last-known* state — that's the correct "as of last verification" data, not garbage.

The lowercase text was a related symptom: rows rendered the **raw lowercased state key** (`breaking.bad.s05.complete…`) — keys are lowercased by design, and v1-era records without cached metadata fell back to them.

## What changed

| Fix | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Display names** | Rows now carry a proper name — cached metadata first, with a **full re-parse fallback** (same titles the Library view shows). Verified live: `The Edge Of Seventeen (2016)`, `#Stuck (2014)` — never the raw key |
| **Auto-refresh** | The queue list re-fetches every 10 s while the tab is open, preserving filters, page, and scroll position — statuses now move along with the engine |
| **Title Case** | Filters (`Any Status`, `Pending`, `Failed`…), table headers (`Status · Item · Info · Attempts`), pagination (`← Prev` / `Next →`), and the row button (`Detail`) all capitalized |

One note: a few odd rows like `Ed 01` / `Op 03` are genuinely ambiguous files (anime credit reels named `ED 01.mp4` with no show context to parse) — the parser can't invent a show name for them; they'll get proper context once the running scan backfills their metadata.

**Refresh once** to pick up the new page. Service restarted on the new build; the scan continues and tv247 will follow it.

The user asks: "Is it really necessary for the fetch to wait until the walk is completed? Can't they run parallelly?"

Analysis of the current design:
- During a scan, the engine is `running=true` → tv247/scheduled runs can't start (engine busy). The fetch waits for the whole scan.
- Priority items DO run in parallel with scans via mini-runs (drain loop) — that's already parallel.
- But the general fetch queue waits.

Can fetch run DURING the scan? Technically yes — the scan only *reads* the filesystem and updates records; runFetch *modifies* state (marks done) and writes .srt files. Conflicts:
1. Both mutate `state.files` — but JS single-threaded; runFetch's await points and the scanner's sync classify chunk interleave safely (no torn state, though logical races: scanner might overwrite a "done" marking? Scanner only sets covered/pending based on disk state; if engine just downloaded, the sidecar exists on disk → scanner sees it → covered ✓ consistent. If scanner classified BEFORE download (mtime unchanged since...) — the scanner sets `p.meta = metaC` and status transitions guarded by coverMtime — a file the engine marks done mid-scan: scanner may see pending (no sidecar at its classify moment) → keeps pending; engine marks done → done. So engine-done records survive the scan ✓.
2. The bigger conflict: both hammer the same SMB link — scan walk is latency-bound; downloads are network-bound to the internet. Mixing is fine bandwidth-wise (scan = LAN SMB, downloads = WAN). Actually they compete little.

To make serial numbers honest ("#1 = next to be fetched"), the API's ordering should mirror the engine's:
- Priority items first (if any queued),
- then attempts ascending,
- then insertion order (state.files key order — insertion order, which JS objects preserve; `Object.entries` gives that ✓).

  rows.sort((a, b) => (a[1].attempts ?? 0) - (b[1].attempts ?? 0));

Implementation details:

service.mjs queue():
```js
  queue(sp) {
    ...
    const prio = new Set(prioritySet);
    let rows = Object.entries(state.files);
    if (status) ...
    if (type) ...
    if (q) ...
    // mirror the engine's fetch order: priority items first, then fewest
    // attempts, then scan/insertion order (stable sort)
    rows.sort((a, b) =>
      (prio.has(a[0].toLowerCase()) ? 0 : 1) - (prio.has(b[0].toLowerCase()) ? 0 : 1) ||
      (a[1].attempts ?? 0) - (b[1].attempts ?? 0));
    const total = rows.length;
    const offset = (page - 1) * per;
    rows = rows.slice(offset, offset + per);
    return {
      total, page, per,
      items: rows.map(([k, r], i) => ({ n: offset + i + 1, key: k, name: queueLabel(k, r), ...pick(...) })),
    };
  },
```
Note: keys in state.files are already lowercase; prioritySet stores lowercase keys ✓. Also entries passed to runFetch are filtered (pending/failed only) — the queue page shows all statuses; when "any status" is selected, the serial reflects the order among... hmm — mixing done/covered rows into the ordering breaks the "next up" semantics: engine only processes pending/failed. The serial should really be the position within the *serviceable* queue. Options: (a) always sort/order as if only pending+failed existed, assigning serials only to those, leaving other statuses without serial (show "—"); (b) keep serials per filtered view.

Better UX: serial = position in the actual fetch queue = only meaningful for pending/failed. When the user filters (status=pending), serials = global queue positions ✓ meaningful. When "any status" shows everything, numbering all rows 1..N sorted by attempts is misleading (covered items aren't in the queue).

Decision: compute serials over the pending+failed subset (the true queue), always. Items outside (done/covered/parked) get `n: null` → client shows "—". Implementation: 
```js
// build the ordered queue index over serviceable items once
const qOrder = Object.entries(state.files)
  .filter(([k, r]) => r.status === "pending" || r.status === "failed")
  .sort((a, b) => (prio.has(a[0]) ? 0 : 1) - (prio.has(b[0]) ? 0 : 1) || (a[1].attempts ?? 0) - (b[1].attempts ?? 0));
const seq = new Map(qOrder.map(([k], i) => [k, i + 1]));
```
Then each row: `n: seq.get(k) ?? null`. This is O(N log N) per request over 18k entries — fine (~few ms).

BUT: does this ordering MATCH the engine exactly? The engine's runFetch: entries = pending/failed filtered by onlySub → sorted attempts-ascending → priority spliced to front. The engine's insertion order = state.files order ✓ same base. For tv247 runs (only '/tv series/' + skipA7MissedToday), the effective order differs (TV only, a7missed excluded). So "next" depends on which run is active. Perfect fidelity is impossible in one number; the attempts-ordered global queue is the honest general answer. Add the priority-first term ✓. Good enough — document in the reply.

2. **Does the whole filesystem walk run again on service restart? Can we avoid it with persistence?**
   Current behavior: on boot, state.json is loaded (scannedAt from last completed scan). The scheduler's stale check: scans only when >20h stale. The ENGINE (runFetch) with skipRescan doesn't rescan. ```js
function nextFetchInfo() {
  if (engine.fetching) return { running: true };
  const now = new Date();
  const today = now.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  const [hh, mm] = (cfg.schedule?.time ?? "13:05").split(":").map(Number);
  const dueNow = (now.getHours() > hh || (now.getHours() === hh && now.getMinutes() >= mm)) && lastScheduledDay !== today;
  const tv247On = cfg.schedule?.tv247 !== false && cfg.schedule?.enabled !== false;
  let tv = null;
  if (tv247On) {
    const backoff = lastTvRunDone > 0 ? 30e3 : lastTvRunStopped ? 2 * 60e3 : 3 * 3600e3;
    tv = lastTvRunEnd + backoff;
  }
  // daily slot (today if still ahead, else tomorrow)
  const dailyAt = new Date(now); dailyAt.setHours(hh, mm, 0, 0);
  if (dailyAt <= now || lastScheduledDay === today) dailyAt.setDate(dailyAt.getDate() + 1);
  const candidates = [];
  if (dueNow) candidates.push({ at: now.toISOString(), kind: "daily" });
  if (tv247On && tv) candidates.push({ at: new Date(tv).toISOString(), kind: "tv247" });
  candidates.push({ at: dailyAt.toISOString(), kind: "daily" });
  candidates.sort((a, b) => new Date(a.at) - new Date(b.at));
  return candidates[0];
}
```

# Done — the countdown now tracks the actual item cadence (pushed, `7995d3d`)

While a fetch run is active, the top bar counts down to the **next item**, not the next run:

```
● Subtitle Fetcher  fetching · macgyver…  next item in 00:04
```

## How it works

- The engine times every item completion and keeps a **rolling average** of the gaps (currently **~6.2 s** on your library — misses are fast, downloads slower, so the average adapts as the mix changes)
- `status()` exposes `nextItemAt = lastCompletion + avgGap`; the header ticks down to it every second
- **Each download/miss fires a status snapshot with a fresh anchor** — so the countdown resets right after every item lands, exactly as you described. When it hits zero it reads "next item due now…" until the next completion arrives
- Long quiet stretches (deferral sweeps) don't pollute the average — gaps over 60 s refresh the anchor without touching it
- Outside runs, it falls back to the run-level countdown (tv247 cycle / daily 13:05)

───── ASSISTANT · 2026-09-01 05:30:46 ─────

· (thinking) The user interrupted my diagnosis. Their question now: their PC's LAN MAC address was `08-BF-B8-B8-7E-4D` (with a DHCP reservation on the TP-Link router), but now the PC shows MAC `DE:46:E7:E8:43:A8`, so the router assigned a random DHCP IP. How did that happen?

This is a **randomized MAC address** — a Windows feature. Windows 10/11 has "Random hardware addresses" (MAC randomization) which can be enabled:
1. **Per-network**: Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi → (network) → "Random hardware addresses" — but that's for Wi-Fi.
2. For **Ethernet**: Windows 11 (22H2+) introduced MAC randomization for Ethernet too?? Actually — Windows 11 has "Random hardware addresses" setting for Wi-Fi primarily. For Ethernet, some adapters/drivers support it.

Key insight from their MAC: `08-BF-B8-B8-7E-4D` vs `DE:46:E7:E8:43:A8`. The first octet of the NEW MAC: DE = 1101 1110 — the second-least-significant bit of the first octet (bit 1, the "locally administered" bit) — 0xDE = 1101 1110: bit 0 (0xFE vs...) let me compute: 0xDE = 11011110 binary. The locally-administered bit is the second-lowest bit of the first octet (0x02). 0xDE & 0x02 = 0x02 → SET → locally administered address (randomized), not a vendor OUI. The old 0x08 = 00001000: & 0x02 = 0 → universally administered (real hardware MAC). So the new MAC is clearly a Windows-randomized address.

Why would Ethernet randomize after a reboot?
- **"Random hardware addresses" toggled ON for the connection**: Settings → Network & Internet → [Ethernet or Wi-Fi] → Random hardware addresses = On (or "Change daily"). If set to "daily", every day/reconnect gets a new MAC → new DHCP lease → reservation doesn't match → random IP. 
- The user (or a Windows update, or some privacy tweak/optimizer script) turned it on. Windows sometimes enables this per-network after driver updates or when a network is marked... actually it defaults OFF. But it can also be enabled via the adapter's device properties ("Randomly generate MAC address" / MACAddress property in advanced adapter settings) or by OEM/privacy software.
- Also possible: the NIC driver's advanced property "Network Address" set to a random value by some utility.

The fix:
1. Turn OFF randomization: Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi/Ethernet → "Random hardware addresses" → Off (both the global setting and per-network). For Ethernet via device manager: adapter Advanced properties → "Network Address"/"Locally Administered Address" → set to the original MAC or "Not Present"/default.
2. Then disable/enable the adapter (or reboot) → the real MAC returns → router's DHCP reservation hands back 192.168.0.100.
3. Alternatively: update the router reservation to the new MAC — but better to kill randomization.

PowerShell to find the setting: `Get-NetAdapter | Select Name, MacAddress, ...` shows current. The randomization toggle for Wi-Fi is in the profile; for Ethernet adapters it's the driver property. Let me check the adapter on their PC: Get-NetAdapter, and check the registry/driver property.

## What happened

import fs from "node:fs";
/** the on-disk casing of a video path: state keys are lowercased, so rebuilt
 *  paths have wrong-case tails — resolve the real parent entry instead */
export function trueVideoPath(vPath) {
  const dir = path.dirname(vPath);
  const base = path.basename(vPath);
  try {
    const hit = fs.readdirSync(dir).find(f => f.toLowerCase() === base.toLowerCase());
    return hit ? path.join(dir, hit) : vPath;
  } catch { return vPath; }
}
```

/** state keys are lowercased; a rebuilt path therefore has a wrong-case tail.
 *  Players pair sidecar subtitles by exact filename, so resolve the video's
 *  real on-disk name (one parent-dir read) before writing anything next to it. */
export function trueVideoPath(vPath) {
  const dir = path.dirname(vPath);
  const base = path.basename(vPath);
  try {
    const hit = fs.readdirSync(dir).find(f => f.toLowerCase() === base.toLowerCase());
    return hit ? path.join(dir, hit) : vPath;
  } catch { return vPath; }
}

/** standing rule: a sidecar we own (*.en.srt) whose name doesn't match its
 *  video's exact filename gets renamed to match — players pair sidecars by
 *  exact name */
function repairSidecarCase(v) {
  const dir = path.dirname(v);
  const want = path.basename(v).replace(/\.[^.]+$/, "") + ".en.srt";

  return true;
}

───── ASSISTANT · 2026-09-01 06:18:29 ─────

# Fixed at both ends (pushed, `e44f6ae`)

## 1. The source: subtitles were written from lowercased state keys

State keys are lowercased by design, and the engine built the write path from the reconstructed key — landing `tacoma.fd.s03e01….en.srt` next to `Tacoma.FD.S03E01….mkv`. Since Windows/SMB is case-insensitive, *our* coverage detection never noticed, but players pair sidecars by **exact filename** and skipped them.

**Fix:** a new `trueVideoPath()` helper resolves the video's real on-disk name (one parent-directory read) — the engine's download writes and the swap flow now use it, so **every future subtitle lands with exact casing**.

## 2. The new standing rule: rename mismatches at scan time

Exactly parallel to the `Subs/`-folder rule: during every scan, any `*.en.srt` whose name case-mismatches its video is **renamed in place** to match. The scan-complete event and feed line report the count. First pass today:
